1:
The friends have run out of answers and the field is left to Job. Gill pictures him pausing for Zophar, whose turn it was to rise; none of the three took it up, secretly persuaded perhaps that he was right and unwilling to own it, or startled by what he had just said of the divine majesty, which showed a knowledge quite unlike the man they had suspected. Keil and Delitzsch mark the idiom, the lifting up of a mashal, used of Balaam's oracles in Numbers 23, and say he now remains master of the discourse.

What that word covers is disputed. Wesley gives it in four: his grave and weighty discourse. Henry hears the title of Solomon's proverbs and a root meaning to rule, and catches a note of triumph over opponents now baffled. Clarke follows Parkhurst to the same root and finds the boldness to match, a man treating his friends with little ceremony. Gregory the Great takes the term the other way, as a likeness rather than a victory, refusing to hear in it any musical instrument, since music in mourning is as a tale out of season; Scripture folds mystical matter into plain narration, he says, so that the obscurity may prick the reader toward a deeper sense.

The oath troubles them more than its solemnity does. Gill, citing Jarchi, counts it a true swearing, by the living God as distinct from breathless idols and from deified heroes who were only dead men. But the clause fastened to the name — that God had taken away his judgment — Henry calls speaking hardly and unbecomingly, recalling Elihu's rebuke that God takes away no man's right. Clarke is blunter: a great want of reverence, an irritation bordering on bitterness that cannot be excused, and no man should speak so of his Maker. Ellicott alone reads the words as faith rather than complaint: the sufferings, though unexplained, are laid on him for purposes veiled from him. Wesley splits the difference — God knows his integrity, yet will not plead his cause against his friends.

What he swears to runs inward, Gill presses: not merely that he will spare a neighbour's name, but that he will not speak wickedly of himself by confessing a hypocrisy he cannot find. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the fourth verse is a vow at all, calling it the agreement of a confession already made with the abiding fact; they render its close with Renan, my heart reproaches me for not one of my days. Clarke hears Adam behind the breath in the nostrils, the principle by which dust became a living and rational creature, so the clause means while I live and reason. Henry builds on the same frailty: our breath will not always be in us, so resolutions against sin should be resolutions for life.

Gill is careful about what is refused: not a judgment on his friends' state before God, but their censure and the doctrine under it, that a man's outward circumstances declare him good or bad — agreeing would be to call evil good. Nor will he let the thing held fast be mistaken for a plea at the bar of heaven; no man clings to that who has seen its insufficiency, the only robe answering there being the living Redeemer's. What this sufferer grips is the justice of his cause. Keil and Delitzsch name it tummah, wholeness of character; Henry calls it the conscience and credit of an unbroken life, and makes perseverance in it the best preparative for dying. To silence the heart's reproach when it has cause is to affront God, whose deputy conscience is; to silence it while uprightness stands is to baffle the whisper that asks if thou be the Son of God. Clarke rests where John does: if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God.
7:
Job now turns outward, and the sentence he passes on counterfeit religion measures how far he stands from it. Gill reads the line as a disclaimer: no good man can really wish anyone wicked, and the wish would be needless, since whoever hates the upright is already so — as the Chaldeans and Sabeans had proved on his own herds. Wesley says it in the first person: he abhors the thought of such practice and could devise no heavier mischief for a foe. Henry hears a proverb behind it, cousin to Daniel's word that the dream be to those who hate thee, and draws it out: one would sooner be a beggar, an outlaw, a galley-slave, anything at all, than stand where the ungodly stand in their pomp. Ellicott keeps it cooler: the prosperity is admitted, not envied. Clarke dissents, taking the clause as a demand rather than a wish: let my accuser be proved a lying and perjured man, who has charged me with what he cannot prove.

Over the next word they part company on philology. Gill's chaneph is the religious dissembler, who seems what he is not, professes what he has not, and worships to be seen; his expectation, Job agreeing here with Bildad and Zophar, is the spider's web and the giving up of the ghost, resting on his substance. Clarke calls the English rendering most improper: the Hebrew means a defiled wretch, a rascal who sticks at nothing to gain his ends, here a rogue who made his fortune by overreaching and cheating. Ellicott, rendering the godless, reshapes the question itself: what is his hope, though he get him gain, when God taketh away his soul? Clarke lists the alternatives he will not take — the Chaldee's detractor who gathered the mammon of unrighteousness, the Septuagint's query whether hoping in the Lord will save such a man, Good's conjecture that God should keep him in quiet — and keeps the Authorised reading, hearing in it the words that were in our Lord's eye about gaining the world and losing oneself.

On the taking away Clarke is most vivid: a righteous man yields up his spirit, while this one must have it forced out of the body, afraid of God and death and eternity alike; he borrows Blair's picture of the frantic soul racing round the walls of her clay tenement, shrieking for help at every avenue, begging a little longer to wash away her stains. Henry works the same verse as an audit. The gain is conceded — Jehu got a kingdom by dissembling and the Pharisees many a widow's house — and on it the structure is raised; what collapses is the inference, when external profession and privilege are pleaded and overruled with Depart from me, I know you not.

The last two questions are rhetorical and all treat them so. Gill denies the cry will be heard, the foolish virgins' words returning unanswered, while the same God hears his own people in life and in death; Henry allows one exception, that true repentance is heard at any hour, and otherwise lines up the texts in which prayer is refused — iniquity regarded in the heart, idols set up, an ear turned from the law, the word go to the gods you have served. Delight is the test Henry presses hardest: nobody perseveres in what gives no pleasure, so the pretender slights God in prosperity and curses him in adversity, keeping up worship while it is in fashion or while the hot fit lasts. Gill itemises what cannot be loved — omnipotence able to destroy soul and body, omniscience that reads the covert heart, a holiness the man does not want. Ellicott sets against him the one who asks whom have I in heaven but thee, and notes that this other has no promise to plead and so no assurance of access.
11:
Job sets up as teacher, and each witness renders the formula differently. Gill takes the hand of God for providence rather than nature: the chapter before had displayed creation, and what is promised now is the harder lesson of why the upright are afflicted and the godless left at ease. He adds that the man is no less fit for the office in calamity than in wealth, adversity having been his school. Clarke reads it as a disclaimer of originality — nothing out of his own head, nothing quoted, but speech under divine assistance; he notes the Chaldee's bolder by the prophecy of God, and prefers Good's concerning the dealings of God. Ellicott renders of the hand of God, or what is in God's power. Henry draws a rule from the teacher's position: we must not disdain to learn even from those who are sick and poor, yea, and peevish too, if what they deliver is true and good.

Then ye yourselves have seen it, and the referent divides them sharply. For Keil and Delitzsch this clause is the pivot of the chapter: the emphatic pronoun means not merely all of you but your very selves, and with it Job concedes what he had seemed to deny, that as a rule the oppressor's end is what the three described. What remains false is the application to him, who does not carry the marks. Ellicott takes the sight to be of something else, the power of God just proclaimed. Gill points at the evidence their own eyes had furnished, the ungodly spreading like a green bay tree while better men laboured, the speaker himself a case in front of them. Clarke lingers on the rebuke, hebel tehbalu, which Good turns into why should ye thus babble babblings, and which he would gladly render vanitize vanity if English allowed. Wesley has it in a line: they are vain to condemn an afflicted man.

Whether the verses that follow are Job's at all is Ellicott's question. Some have supposed them the missing third speech of Zophar, the rubric having dropped out; he will not have it, since what the arrangement gains in symmetry it loses in drama — Bildad managed only a few truisms, and it is no wonder that when the turn came round again there was nothing left to say. One thing he grants is a little remarkable, that the speaker takes up precisely the words with which Zophar had closed. The explanation offered is that Job accepts his friends' facts entire while refusing their inference: the prosperity of the godless is seeming rather than real, and on that much they agree.

Henry maps the agreement and the quarrel with care. Both sides hold that cruelty will be reckoned with; what the three maintained, and he cites them verse by verse, was that the reckoning falls visibly and soon — pain all their days, the destroyer in their prosperity, the branch not green, the end before its time. Job's correction is about timing: the stroke is often deferred, and a reprieve is not a pardon. Gill pushes the deferral past death, where the portion is the second death and the company of devils and dissemblers; Clarke keeps a middle course, allowing that the displeasure is often shown where men can see it and at other times held over, lest anyone forget that perdition and recompense are both coming. The first instance turns a blessing into a target. Many children, Gill observes, are common to good and bad — Haman left ten sons and Ahab seventy. Henry sees in a numerous, well-settled family only more and fairer marks for the three arrows of sword, famine and pestilence: war's sword for those bred to live by it, or justice's, or the murderer's for the estate, and for the rest a poverty with neither enough nor what they were used to.
15:
The survivors come first, and the phrase that covers them satisfies nobody. Clarke reads buried in death as the strongest thing the words can carry: death itself is the place where such a man lies, with no redemption and no rising; he rejects the Chaldee's entombed in corruption, which entombs high and low alike. Keil and Delitzsch hear the pestilence in the verb, third of the strokes that fall one after another, and find the clause shared with Asaph's psalm. Ellicott keeps it quieter: the end will be obscure, a death that is itself a burial into oblivion. On the tearless widows they diverge again — Wesley explains the plural by polygamy and the dry eyes by the tyranny endured; Ellicott offers hired mourning-women or the wives of the survivors; Keil and Delitzsch say the blows come too fast for the rites.

Then the hoard, which Gill reads as a portrait of appetite: a man who cannot be content without amassing. Henry watches the heaping until, as James says, the silver is cankered and the garments moth-eaten: death will strip him, and the robe he laid up will be worn by the just while the innocent share out the metal. Providence disposes of estates as it pleases, often making men's wills against their wills — the Egyptians' jewels were Israel's pay — and the new owners spread rather than hoard, money being like manure, good for nothing unless it is spread. Clarke moralises the instrument: of all possessions money is the readiest agent for good or ill, so its abuser is doubly cursed and its right user doubly blessed.

The two images of the dwelling are handled almost alike, their force lying in the detail. Gill lets the moth eat itself out of house and home and be brushed away at last; he notes a rendering making the palace a thing among the stars, and applies it all to a confidence of spider's web, moth-eaten cloth and sand. Clarke admires the skill of the building, then dissolves it: the insect's lodging belongs to the caterpillar state and lasts only until the change, and the watchman's booth, run up of the lightest materials to shade him while the grapes ripen, is left to the winter rains. Wesley has the moth crushed in the garment and the shed pulled down as suddenly as it rose. Henry adds the tenant's security: no apprehension of danger, and his place shall know him no more.

The last verse here is the most contested. Clarke lays out two readings and will not pretend they are one. The first takes the lying down for the grave, where there is neither a respectable interment among men nor a gathering with the righteous; behind it the old notion that the unburied wander and find no rest, and puts the opened eyes at the resurrection morning. The second keeps it in this world: the owner goes to bed sure his property is safe, adds nothing to it, and wakes to find a hostile tribe has carried off the whole — common enough in Arabia, and precisely what had happened to the speaker. Clarke prefers the first, as got without crucifying the text. Ellicott lets the gathering be of the wealth, not the man: he opens his eyes and it is gone. Gill offers a sleepless alternative, the abundance and the fear of losing it refusing to let him settle. Henry develops that into the picture the chapter needs: he lies down in his riches as in a strong city and the world calls him happy, but is full of tossings to and fro till dawn, his cares feeding his fears, so that we follow him to bed and do not find him at ease. Wesley ends bluntly — a carcase like dung instead of an honourable grave with his fathers, his name extinct with him.
20:
Four verses of weather close the discourse: the witnesses agree on the violence and divide on the rest. Gill hears in the flood image both the deathbed and what follows: a guilty memory running back over old sins, the law's curses alighting, the fury of the Almighty surrounding him, devils for company — terror on every side, a Magor-missabib, rolling on without ceasing. Clarke keeps to the tempest in the night, where darkness half hides the danger and the way out. Wesley gives the simile a river breaking its banks, the wrath coming unexpectedly, like a thief. Henry splits the reaction in two: terror produces either a silent and sullen despair, in which the storm steals the man away at night with nobody aware of it, or an open and clamorous one, in which he is hurled from his place with noise; death being a fair gale to carry the godly home and an east wind to hurry the other off.

On that wind Keil and Delitzsch are most informative. The qadim out of the Arabian desert is the destructive and parching wind of the language, and goes now by another name, the wind from the sunrise; rare in summer and frequent in winter, it burns up the young growth if it holds, and a year of famine follows, which is why Lebanon calls it by a word that has come to mean poisonous but first meant devastating. They add what it does to a body: blood excited, chest contracted, restlessness and bad dreams, man and beast feeling sickly while it lasts. Gill prefers the burning wind of the Septuagint and Vulgate, quoting Thevenot for the blast that gives a man time only to say he burns before he drops. Clarke names it with a sailor's word, a levanter, the euroclydon that wrecked Paul.

Then the chapter's sharpest division, over who does the casting. The Authorised reading supplies God, and Gill fills it out: sins laid on the conscience as an intolerable weight, wrath poured like fire, punishment pressing like a talent of lead, and no sparing from one who spared neither the sinning angels nor the old world nor Sodom. Henry works the same thought: no flying from what is cast down and no bearing up under it, the gates locked, the gulf fixed, rocks and mountains vainly called on for shelter; those who will not flee now to the arms of grace will not be able to flee from the arms of wrath. Wesley repeats that sentence almost word for word and takes the casting for darts or plagues one after another. Ellicott dissents: the subject may be the man who spent his life fleeing from the tyrant's power and is now only too glad to avenge himself. Clarke goes further and would delete the supplied subject, keeping the storm of the verses before as the agent: it shall fall on him and not spare, and flying from its power he shall continue to fly.

The hands and the hiss end it, read at three different distances. Clarke personifies the weather to the last, letting the storm clap and shriek the man off the stage, and explains the gesture from an old practice of hissing an officer out of a post he has disgraced. Wesley reads it of onlookers: joy at the removal of a public pest, astonishment, and plain contempt. Henry has the judgments applauded and the name left with perpetual marks of infamy: where he was caressed and cried up he shall be laughed at, and his ashes trampled. Gill will not let the clapping be cruelty. The righteous take no pleasure in the scene and indulge no evil passion; what they rejoice in is the glory of justice. He would widen the company to the angels, or read the verb impersonally, so the hands clapped are justice's own triumph rather than anybody's spite.
